messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Writer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was twenty years old when his younger brother Ravi drowned during a family trip to a reservoir two summers ago. Ravi had waded in past the drop-off and disappeared so quickly that Arjun still could not believe it when he thinks about the sequence—the splash, the seconds of silence, the cold panic as he thrashed through the water and clawed at nothing. He held Ravi’s wrist for a moment before the current pulled the body away; it slipped out of his hand like a fish. Afterwards, when he closed his eyes at night, that exact sensation of the wrist sliding through his fingers replayed in full sensory detail, and his stomach would drop as if he were falling himself.

In the months that followed, Arjun stopped being able to sit still. He had always written in coffee shops or on the fire escape of his apartment, letting the street noise blur into background static, but now every unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a dropped tray in a café, the rattle of a window shade—made him flinch so violently that people would stare. He started working from home exclusively, though the safety of his own desk offered no relief; he lay on the floor at night with his heart pounding at creaks he knew were harmless, unable to trust the fact that the door was locked and the radiator was just clicking. Sleep, when it came, was shallow and stained with fragments of the reservoir, and he would wake up multiple times, drenched and disoriented, checking his phone for messages that weren’t coming.

He had been a writer of short fiction, a bright young voice in his workshop group, but the sentences now felt like lies. His characters needed futures, and the idea of planning even a few paragraphs ahead made his throat tighten. Making any plan for his own life felt worse: scheduling a dentist appointment, agreeing to meet a friend next week, even thinking about his birthday. Every time he tried, a voice inside him said, *You don’t know that you’ll still be here. You don’t know that nothing will happen.* He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place—not abstractly dangerous, but actively watching for a moment of careless hope. The same mechanism that had let Ravi slip under the water could take anything, anyone, anytime. He called his mother three or four times a day, not to talk but to ask, point-blank, “Are you sure you’re okay? You’d tell me if something was wrong, right?” She would reassure him, but the reassurance dissolved within minutes, and he would call again, hating himself for the need.

The grief reminders were everywhere: Ravi’s favorite sneakers still by the door, the Indian takeout place they always ordered from, a certain radio station that played the songs Ravi hummed. Arjun stopped taking that bus route, deleted the takeout app, moved the sneakers to a closet he never opened. But the most insidious reminders were the ones he could not avoid—sunlight on water, the smell of lake air, a child’s laugh that sounded like Ravi’s. Each one sent him into a spiral of misery that he could not shake. He used to be a happy person; his friends remembered him as the one who told stupid jokes and stayed up late trading story ideas. Now he felt hollow, convinced that the old Arjun had drowned alongside his brother and left this bitter, jumpy shell behind. His beliefs about how the world worked had been destroyed: he no longer trusted that good things lasted, that effort mattered, that people died in old age after full lives.

The consequence was slow and concrete. He stopped submitting to journals, stopped responding to his editor, stopped showing up to workshop. His last piece had been due eight months ago. His parents flew out from Chicago to see him and found an apartment with unwashed dishes, a laptop covered in dust, and a son who could not meet their eyes. At their urging, he finally agreed to see a therapist, mostly because he was too tired to argue. Sitting in the waiting room now, he is terrified that talking about it will make the memories sharper, but he is also, somewhere underneath the vigilance, dimly aware that he does not want to spend the rest of his life flinching at a closing door.
